text: A mammal, derived from the Latin *mamma* meaning "breast," is a vertebrate belonging to the class Mammalia, characterised by milk-producing mammary glands, a broad neocortex, fur or hair, and three middle ear bones. These traits distinguish mammals from reptiles and birds, whose ancestors diverged from them during the Carboniferous Period over 300 million years ago. Approximately 6,640 extant species of mammals have been described and are divided into 27 orders. The largest orders by species count are Rodentia (including mice, rats, porcupines, beavers, capybaras), Chiroptera (bats), and Eulipotyphla (including hedgehogs, moles, and shrews). The next three are Primates (including humans, monkeys, and lemurs), Cetartiodactyla (including pigs, bovids, and whales), and Carnivora (including cats, dogs, and seals). Mammals are the only living members of Synapsida, a clade that, along with Sauropsida (reptiles and birds), forms the larger Amniota group. Early synapsids, known as pelycosaurs, evolved during the Pennsylvanian subperiod (~323 to ~300 million years ago), splitting from the reptile lineage. Therapsids, which emerged in the Middle Permian (~265 million years ago), became dominant land vertebrates and gave rise to mammals through a series of evolutionary stages culminating in cynodonts. Mammals originated from cynodonts during the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, with the first known mammals (in Kemp's definition) appearing around 225 million years ago. Crown group mammals evolved from earlier mammaliaforms during the Early Jurassic. The modern diversity of mammals developed in the Paleogene and Neogene periods of the Cenozoic era after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs, making mammals the dominant terrestrial group since 66 million years ago. Most mammals are quadrupedal, though some have adapted for life in water, air, trees, or underground; bipeds use only the lower limbs, while cetaceans and sea cows have reduced rear limbs. Mammals range in size from the 30–40 millimetres (1.2–1.6 inches) bumblebee bat to the 30-metre (98-foot) blue whale, the largest animal ever known. Lifespan varies from two years in shrews to 211 years in the bowhead whale. All modern mammals give birth to live young, except the five monotreme species, which lay eggs. The most species-rich group is viviparous placental mammals, which use a placenta to nourish offspring during gestation. Most mammals are intelligent, with some exhibiting large brains, self-awareness, and tool use; they communicate through vocalisations, ultrasound, scent marking, alarm signals, singing, echolocation, and in humans, complex language. Mammals form fission–fusion societies, harems, or hierarchies, though some are solitary and territorial, and most are polygynous, though some are monogamous or polyandrous. Domestication of mammals during the Neolithic Revolution shifted human societies from nomadic to sedentary, enabling farming and leading to the development of early civilisations. Domesticated mammals provide transport, agriculture, food (meat and dairy), fur, and leather, and are also used for sport, as pets, working animals, and in scientific research. Mammals have been depicted in art since the Paleolithic and appear in literature, film, mythology, and religion. Declines in numbers and extinctions are primarily due to human poaching and habitat destruction, especially deforestation. Mammal classification has evolved since Carl Linnaeus first defined the class in 1758, and no system is universally accepted; McKenna & Bell (1997) and Wilson & Reeder (2005) offer useful compendiums, while Simpson (1945) was widely taught until the end of the 20th century. However, since 1945, new paleontological data and cladistic methods have challenged Simpson’s classification, which remains the closest to an official system despite its flaws. Most mammals, including the six most species-rich orders, belong to the placental group. According to Mammal Species of the World, 5,416 species were identified in 2006, grouped into 1,229 genera, 153 families, and 29 orders; by 2008, the IUCN counted 5,488 species in its Global Mammal Assessment. Research published in the Journal of Mammalogy in 2018 identified 6,495 mammal species, including 96 recently extinct. The term "mammal" is modern, coined by Linnaeus in 1758 from *mamma*. Timothy Rowe (1988) defined Mammalia as the crown group—the most recent common ancestor of living monotremes (echidnas and platypuses) and therians (marsupials and placentals), and all descendants—dating its origin to the Jurassic Period, around 167 million years ago, based on fossils like Ambondro, Amphilestes, and Amphitherium. T. S. Kemp defines mammals as synapsids with a dentary–squamosal jaw articulation and transverse molar occlusion, with the earliest known example, Tikitherium, dating to 225 million years ago. Molecular studies based on DNA and retrotransposon data suggest three major placental lineages—Afrotheria, Xenarthra, and Boreoeutheria—diverging in the Cretaceous, with divergence times ranging from 105 to 120 million years ago depending on DNA type and paleogeographic interpretations. The relationships among these groups remain contentious, with hypotheses including Atlantogenata, Epitheria, and Exafroplacentalia. Boreoeutheria includes Euarchontoglires and Laurasiatheria. Phylogeny according to Álvarez-Carretero et al. (2022) includes Monotremata, Paucituberculata, Didelphimorphia, Microbiotheria, Notoryctemorphia, Peramelemorphia, Dasyuromorphia, Diprotodontia, Cingulata, Pilosa, Hyracoidea, Sirenia, Proboscidea, Tubulidentata, Macroscelidea, Afrosoricida, Eulipotyphla, Chiroptera, Pholidota, Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Scandentia, Lagomorpha, Rodentia, Dermoptera, and Primates. The first fully terrestrial vertebrates were amniotes, which evolved from amphibious tetrapods in the Pennsylvanian and had internal membranes allowing egg development on land. Two major amniote lineages emerged: Synapsida (including mammals) and Sauropsida (including reptiles, birds, and dinosaurs). Synapsids have a single temporal fenestra; early forms like Dimetrodon were large and predatory. Nonmammalian synapsids were incorrectly called "mammal-like reptiles" but are neither reptiles nor part of the reptile lineage. Therapsids evolved in the Middle Permian and became dominant. The Permian–Triassic extinction event (~252 million years ago) ended carnivorous therapsid dominance, with archosaurs (crocodiles, pterosaurs, dinosaurs) taking over large carnivore niches. Large cynodonts like Trucidocynodon and traversodontids still occupied herbivorous and carnivorous roles. By the Jurassic, dinosaurs dominated large herbivore niches. Mammals expanded from a nocturnal insectivore niche from the mid-Jurassic onward; Castorocauda, a Jurassic relative, had adaptations for swimming and digging. Most mammals remained nocturnal, contributing to their traits. Mesozoic mammal species were mostly multituberculates, eutriconodonts, and spalacotheriids. The earliest known metatherian, Sinodelphys, dates to 125 million years ago in China and includes fur and soft tissue imprints. The earliest known eutherian, Juramaia sinensis, is from 160 million years ago in the late Jurassic. Eomaia, from 125 million years ago, shares features with marsupials but not placentals, including epipubic bones extending from the pelvis—present in marsupials, monotremes, and early eutherians like Asioryctitheria but absent in modern placentals. These bones stiffen muscles and reduce pelvic space, suggesting a short gestation and small newborns, indicating the placenta evolved later. Epipubic bones are ancestral and lost in placental mammals. One of the earliest monotremes, Teinolophos, lived about 120 million years ago in Australia. Monotremes retain a cloaca (shared orifice for urination, defecation, and reproduction) and lay leathery, uncalcified eggs. Hadrocodium, from 195 million years ago in the early Jurassic, shows the first clear jaw joint formed solely by the dentary and squamosal bones, with no articular bone. The earliest clear evidence of hair or fur comes from Castorocauda and Megaconus, from 164 million years ago. In the 1950s, foramina in cynodont jaws were thought to indicate whiskers and fur, but modern lizards like Tupinambis have similar foramina without whiskers, so this evidence is not definitive. Studies of Permian coprolites suggest non-mammalian synapsids had fur, possibly as early as dicynodonts. Endothermy likely first evolved in non-mammalian therapsids. Monotremes have lower body temperatures and variable metabolic rates than marsupials and placentals, though some ancestors may have had therian-like body temperatures. Some modern therians, like afrotheres and xenarthrans, have secondarily evolved lower body temperatures. Erect limbs evolved incompletely—monotremes have sprawling limbs—while parasagittal limb posture appeared in the late Jurassic or early Cretaceous in eutherian Eomaia and metatherian Sinodelphys, both dated to 125 million years ago. Epipubic bones are a feature present in early mammals and lost in placentals.

Studies on Permian coprolites indicate that non-mammalian synapsids of that epoch already possessed fur, suggesting the evolution of hairs may have originated as early as in dicynodonts. The origin of endothermy in mammals is uncertain, though it is generally believed to have first evolved in non-mammalian therapsids. Modern monotremes have lower body temperatures and more variable metabolic rates than marsupials and placentals, but evidence suggests some of their ancestors, possibly including those of therians, may have had body temperatures similar to modern therians. Some modern therians, such as afrotheres and xenarthrans, have secondarily evolved lower body temperatures. The evolution of erect limbs in mammals is incomplete—both living and fossil monotremes have sprawling limbs. The parasagittal (nonsprawling) limb posture emerged during the late Jurassic or early Cretaceous and is found in eutherian Eomaia and metatherian Sinodelphys, both dated to 125 million years ago. Epipubic bones, a trait influential in mammal reproduction, first appear in Tritylodontidae and are considered a synapomorphy between them and Mammaliaformes; they are widespread in non-placental Mammaliaformes, though Megazostrodon and Erythrotherium appear to lack them. It is proposed that the original function of lactation was to keep eggs moist, primarily based on observations of monotremes. In human females, mammary glands develop fully during puberty regardless of pregnancy. Therians occupied medium- to large-sized ecological niches in the Cenozoic after the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event about 66 million years ago, which eliminated ecological space previously held by non-avian dinosaurs and other reptiles, leading to an exponential increase in body size (megafauna). This diversification was not solely due to expansion into large-bodied niches; mammals diversified rapidly, showing an exponential rise in diversity. For instance, the earliest-known bat dates to about 50 million years ago, only 16 million years after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. Molecular phylogenetic studies initially suggested most placental orders diverged between 100 and 85 million years ago, with modern families emerging from the late Eocene through the Miocene, though no placental fossils have been found before the end of the Cretaceous. The earliest undisputed placental fossils come from the early Paleocene, after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs; Protungulatum donnae was once considered one of the first placental mammals but has since been reclassified as a non-placental eutherian. Recalibrations of genetic and morphological diversity rates suggest a Late Cretaceous origin for placentals and a Paleocene origin for most modern clades. The earliest-known ancestor of primates is Archicebus achilles, dating to around 55 million years ago, weighing 20–30 grams and fitting within a human palm. Living mammals are identified by the presence of sweat glands, including those specialized for milk production, though in fossil classification, other features are used due to the absence of soft tissue. Many traits shared by all living mammals appeared in the earliest members of the group, which were not present in Triassic mammal ancestors. Nearly all mammaliaforms possess an epipubic bone, with modern placentals being the exception. On average, male mammals are larger than females, with males being at least 10% larger in over 45% of species; most orders show male-biased sexual dimorphism, though some, like Lagomorpha, show no bias or are female-biased. Sexual size dimorphism increases with body size (Rensch's rule), with male-biased dimorphism linked to male–male competition and sexual selection, which correlates with mating systems and both male and female size. Female mass is also under parallel selection, with higher weaning age in polygynous species and lower fecundity in larger females, indicating selection for smaller females. These patterns hold across mammals, though there is variation among orders. Most mammals have seven cervical vertebrae; exceptions include the manatee and two-toed sloth (six) and the three-toed sloth (nine). All mammals have a neocortex, a brain region unique to mammals. Placental brains have a corpus callosum, unlike monotremes and marsupials. The mammalian heart has four chambers—two atria and two ventricles—with four valves ensuring unidirectional blood flow. Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left atrium via pulmonary veins and flows into the left ventricle, with most blood entering passively during relaxation, and the left atrium contracting near the end of ventricular relaxation to pump blood. The heart is supplied with nutrients and oxygen via coronary arteries. Mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus to accommodate more hemoglobin, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. Mammalian lungs are spongy and honeycombed, with breathing primarily driven by the diaphragm, which contracts to increase thoracic volume and relaxes to decrease it, expelling air. During exercise, abdominal muscles contract to increase pressure on the diaphragm, forcing air out more forcefully. The rib cage expands and contracts via respiratory muscles, allowing air to move down its pressure gradient. This system is known as a bellows lung. The integumentary system consists of three layers: epidermis (10–30 cells thick, providing waterproofing), dermis (15–40 times thicker, containing blood vessels and bones), and hypodermis (adipose tissue for insulation and cushioning; thickness varies, with right whales having the thickest at 20 inches or 51 cm). No other animals have hair, which is a definitive mammalian trait, though some have very little. Herbivores have evolved diverse dental structures for plant consumption: frugivores and soft-leaf feeders have low-crowned teeth for grinding; grazers with silica-rich grasses have high-crowned teeth that wear less. Carnivores have carnassial teeth, long canines, and similar tooth replacement patterns. Even-toed ungulates (Artiodactyla) have a four-chambered stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum), where plant material is mixed with saliva, separated, and regurgitated as cud; cellulolytic microbes break down cellulose. Perissodactyls store digested food in an enlarged cecum for fermentation. Carnivores have a simple stomach adapted for meat digestion, with a short or absent cecum and a non-sacculated large intestine. Mammals are ureotelic, converting ammonia to urea via the liver's urea cycle; bilirubin, a byproduct of blood cells, is excreted through bile and urine, giving feces a brown color. Mammalian kidneys have a renal pelvis, pyramids, cortex, and medulla due to elongated loops of Henle; they are typically bean-shaped, though pinnipeds, cetaceans, and bears have multilobed kidneys. Most adult placentals lack a cloaca; in embryos, the cloaca divides into a posterior region becoming the anus and an anterior region that develops into the urogenital sinus in females or the penile urethra in males. Afrosoricids and some shrews retain a cloaca as adults; marsupials have a separate genital tract with a trace of the cloaca externally; monotremes have a true cloaca, with urine flowing into it rather than a bladder in placentals. Mammals have a larynx that opens and closes quickly to produce sounds, with a supralaryngeal vocal tract filtering sound. The lungs and surrounding muscles provide air and pressure for phonation. More primitive mammals like echidnas produce only hisses through exhalation; other mammals use vocal folds to generate sounds such as purring and screaming. Mammals can shift the larynx to breathe through the nose while swallowing through the mouth and produce oral or nasal sounds; nasal sounds are soft, oral sounds are loud. Some mammals, like the hammer-headed bat (Hypsignathus monstrosus), have a large larynx that occupies the thoracic cavity, lowering pitch; large vocal pads, such as in big cats, also lower pitch. Infrasound is produced by elephants and baleen whales; small mammals with small larynxes produce ultrasound, detectable via middle ear and cochlear modifications, used in mother-to-pup communication and echolocation in bats and toothed whales, which use a melon instead of a vocal membrane. Primates have air sacs attached to the larynx that may lower resonances or increase sound volume. Vocal production is controlled by cranial nerve nuclei in the brain, supplied by the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves (branches of the vagus), and the hypoglossal and facial nerves; electrical stimulation of the periaqueductal grey (PEG) region elicits vocalizations. The ability to learn new vocalizations is found only in humans, seals, cetaceans, elephants, and possibly bats, with humans having a direct connection between the motor cortex and spinal motor neurons. The primary function of fur is thermoregulation, with additional roles in protection, sensory functions, waterproofing, and camouflage. Hair length does not affect thermoregulation; for example, tropical mammals like sloths have similar fur length to arctic mammals but less insulation, while some tropical mammals with short hair have the same insulating value as arctic mammals. Fur denseness increases insulation, with arctic mammals like the musk ox having dense underfur and guard hairs up to 30 cm long, forming an airtight coat to survive −40°C. Desert mammals like camels use dense fur to block solar heat, with fur reaching 70°C while skin stays at 40°C. Aquatic mammals trap air in fur to conserve heat by keeping skin dry. Mammalian coat coloration is influenced by camouflage, sexual selection, communication, and thermoregulation, primarily due to melanin types: eumelanin for brown and black, pheomelanin for yellow to reddish hues. Some mammals, such as mandrills, vervet monkeys, and certain opossums, have blue skin due to light diffraction in collagen. Many sloths appear green because their fur hosts green algae, possibly a symbiotic relationship aiding camouflage. Camouflage is significant in many mammals, such as arctic foxes, collared lemmings, stoats, and snowshoe hares, which change color seasonally from brown in summer to white in winter. Arboreal mammals like primates and marsupials have violet, green, or blue skin, indicating adaptive advantages in arboreal habitats. Aposematism is mentioned.

Some mammals exhibit vibrant colors due to light diffraction in collagen fibers, such as mandrills, vervet monkeys, Mexican mouse opossums, and Derby's woolly opossums, which have blue skin. Many sloths appear green because their fur hosts green algae, possibly indicating a symbiotic relationship that provides camouflage. Camouflage is a significant factor in many mammals, helping them avoid predators or prey; for instance, arctic and subarctic mammals like the arctic fox (Alopex lagopus), collared lemming (Dicrostonyx groenlandicus), stoat (Mustela erminea), and snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus) change color seasonally—being brown in summer and white in winter—to match their environment. Arboreal mammals, including primates and marsupials, often have violet, green, or blue skin, suggesting an evolutionary advantage in tree-dwelling habitats through convergent evolution. Aposematism, or warning coloration, explains the black-and-white pelage of self-defense species like skunks and honey badgers. Coat color can be sexually dimorphic in many primates, with differences potentially reflecting nutrition and hormone levels relevant to mate selection. Darker coats absorb more solar radiation and help retain heat, with some small mammals like voles having darker fur in winter; in contrast, arctic mammals such as the polar bear have white, pigmentless fur that reflects solar radiation. The black-and-white striping of zebras may deter biting flies. Mammals reproduce through internal fertilization and are solely gonochoric, meaning individuals are born with either male or female genitalia. Males ejaculate semen through a penis, which may be enclosed in a prepuce, and some placentals urinate through the penis; some also possess a penis bone (baculum). Marsupials typically have forked penises, while echidna penises have four heads with only two functional. Erection can result from blood flow into spongy tissue or muscular action. Most mammals have testicles that descend into the scrotum, usually located posterior to the penis, though in marsupials it is often anterior. Females generally have a vulva (clitoris and labia) externally, with internal structures including paired oviducts, one or two uteri, one or two cervices, and a vagina; marsupials have two lateral vaginas and a medial vagina, while monotreme "vagina" is better described as a urogenital sinus. Placental uterine systems vary: duplex (two uteri and cervices), bipartite (two uterine horns with one cervix), bicornuate (Y-shaped), or simplex (single uterus). The ancestral mammalian reproductive condition involves giving birth to relatively undeveloped young, either via direct vivipary or short-lived soft-shelled eggs, likely due to epipubic bones restricting torso expansion. Kayentatherium, an early mammal, produced undeveloped perinates in litters of 38. Most modern mammals are viviparous, but the five monotreme species—platypus and four echidna species—lay eggs. Monotremes have a sex-determination system distinct from most mammals, with platypus sex chromosomes resembling those of chickens. Marsupials have a short gestation period, giving birth to underdeveloped young that continue developing in a pouch (marsupium), a plesiomorphic trait among viviparous mammals due to epipubic bones preventing torso expansion; even non-placental eutherians likely reproduced this way. Placentals give birth to more developed young after long gestation periods, thanks to the placenta, which connects the fetus to the uterine wall for nutrient exchange. In placentals, epipubic bones are either lost or transformed into the baculum, enabling torso expansion. Most mammals give birth multiple times in their lifespan, though a few are semelparous. Mammalian mammary glands produce milk, the primary nutrition for newborns; monotremes lack teats but have mammary glands, with young licking milk from patches on the mother’s belly. Marsupial milk changes in production and composition due to underdeveloped young, and mammary glands have autonomy to supply different milks at various developmental stages. Placental milk is dominated by lactose, while monotreme and marsupial milk is dominated by oligosaccharides. Weaning occurs when a mammal reduces dependence on maternal milk and transitions to solid food. Nearly all mammals are endothermic ("warm-blooded"), with hair aiding in thermoregulation, allowing them to forage in cold climates where ectothermic animals cannot survive. Endothermy requires high food intake, so mammals consume more per unit of body weight than reptiles; small insectivorous mammals eat large amounts, while the naked mole-rat produces little metabolic heat and is considered an operational poikilotherm. Birds are also endothermic, so endothermy is not unique to mammals. Mammalian lifespan varies widely—from one year in the yellow-sided opossum to 211 years in the oldest bowhead whale. DNA repair capacity is strongly linked to lifespan; a 1974 study by Hart and Setlow found that DNA excision repair increases with species lifespan, and species with longer lifespans show better recognition of DNA double-strand breaks and higher levels of the Ku80 protein. In a study of 16 mammalian species, DNA repair genes were up-regulated in longer-lived species, and the cellular level of poly ADP ribose polymerase correlated with lifespan in 13 species. Additional studies across various mammalian species also found a correlation between lifespan and DNA repair capability. Most vertebrates walk plantigrade, but many mammals like cats and dogs are digitigrade, walking on their toes for greater speed. Horses are unguligrade, walking on the tips of their toes for increased stride length and speed. Great apes, giant anteaters, and platypuses are knuckle-walkers. Some mammals, such as humans and great apes, are bipedal, using two limbs for locomotion, which provides a wider field of vision, energy conservation, and hand manipulation for foraging; some bipeds hop, such as kangaroos and kangaroo rats. Animals use different gaits depending on speed, terrain, and situation; horses have four natural gaits: walk, trot, canter, and gallop, with occasional unusual gaits like crawling. Quadrupeds use gaits categorized by support sequence: walking (some feet on ground), running (all feet off ground at some point), and leaping. Arboreal mammals often have elongated limbs to cross gaps, reach food, or brachiate; many, such as tree porcupines, silky anteaters, spider monkeys, and possums, have prehensile tails for grasping branches. Spider monkeys have adhesive pads or bare patches at the tail tip for increased friction. Claws help with climbing rough surfaces and reorienting forces, enabling squirrels to climb large, flat tree trunks, though they can interfere with grasping small branches. Primates use hairless fingertips to grip branches via friction, with grip strength depending on branch diameter. Squirrels have mobile ankle joints that allow them to rotate their feet into a reversed posture, enabling claws to hook into bark and counteract gravity. Small size offers advantages to arboreal species, including larger relative branch size, lower center of mass, increased stability, lower mass, and better movement in cluttered habitats. Size affects gliding animals like sugar gliders. Some primates, bats, and sloths achieve passive stability by hanging beneath branches, making pitching and tipping irrelevant. Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, using wing movements to generate lift and thrust. Their wings are thinner and contain more bones than birds, allowing greater maneuverability and lift with less drag. By folding wings during upstrokes, bats use 35% less energy than birds. Bat wing membranes are delicate but can regenerate small tears. Touch-sensitive receptors called Merkel cells, with tiny hairs in the center, are present on bat wings, enhancing sensitivity to airflow and enabling efficient flight through wing shape adjustments. Fossorial mammals, adapted to digging, include badgers, naked mole-rats, and many rodents; they live primarily underground, with subterranean species living exclusively underground and sub-fossorial species having limited adaptations. Fossorial mammals have fusiform bodies, thick at the shoulders and tapering at the tail and nose, with degenerated eyes (e.g., fully fossorial marsupial moles have useless eyes, while pocket gophers have small functional eyes); external ears are small or absent. They have short, stout legs for strength over speed, broad front paws with strong claws for digging, and webbed back paws with claws to throw dirt backward; most have large incisors to prevent dirt from entering their mouths. Shrews, hedgehogs, and moles were once classified under the obsolete order Insectivora. Fully aquatic mammals, such as cetaceans and sirenians, have lost their legs and use tail fins for propulsion; whales move their tail fins up and down for forward motion, with flippers used for steering; most have dorsal fins to prevent flipping. Sirenians move using flukes raised and lowered in long strokes, which can be twisted for turning, with paddle-like forelimbs aiding in turning and slowing. Semi-aquatic mammals, such as pinnipeds, have two pairs of flippers (fore and hind), with elbows and ankles enclosed; they reduce drag through streamlined bodies, smooth muscle bundles, and lack of arrector pili allowing fur to be streamlined. Fore-flippers are used for locomotion in a wing-like manner, with movement not continuous and gliding between strokes; reduced fore-limb length provides mechanical advantage at the shoulder and elbow joints, while hind-flippers serve as stabilizers. Other semi-aquatic mammals include beavers, hippos, otters, and platypuses. Hippos are large semi-aquatic mammals with barrel-shaped bodies and graviportal skeletal structures adapted to support their weight; their specific gravity allows them to sink and move along river bottoms. Many mammals communicate through vocalizations for mating, warning, food signaling, and social interaction. Males often call during mating to attract females and deter rivals, such as lions and red deer roaring. Humpback whale songs may signal to females and vary by region, forming distinct dialects. Social vocalizations include territorial calls.

The animal glides between each stroke, and compared to terrestrial carnivorans, its fore-limbs are reduced in length, providing greater mechanical advantage to the locomotor muscles at the shoulder and elbow joints; the hind-flippers function as stabilizers. Other semi-aquatic mammals include beavers, hippopotamuses, otters, and platypuses. Hippos are large semi-aquatic mammals with barrel-shaped bodies that have graviportal skeletal structures adapted to support their massive weight, and their specific gravity allows them to sink and move along the riverbed. Mammals communicate through vocalizations for purposes such as mating rituals, warning calls, indicating food sources, and social interaction. Males often call during mating to deter rivals and attract females, as seen in lions and red deer; humpback whale songs may signal to females and vary by ocean region; gibbons use territorial calls, and greater spear-nosed bats use frequency to distinguish groups; vervet monkeys emit distinct alarm calls for at least four predators, triggering different responses—such as climbing trees for a python or seeking ground cover for an eagle—and prairie dogs produce complex calls indicating predator type, size, and speed. Elephants use a range of sounds including snorting, screaming, trumpeting, roaring, and rumbling, some of which are infrasonic and can travel up to 6 miles (9.7 km) during still times near sunrise or sunset. Many mammals use visual anti-predator signals, such as deer and gazelle stotting to show fitness or white-tailed deer flagging their tails when alarmed to alert predators. Scent-marking is used by many mammals, likely for territorial defense and various social functions. Microbats and toothed whales, including oceanic dolphins, use vocalizations for both social interaction and echolocation. Maintaining a high body temperature is energetically costly, so mammals require a nutritious and abundant diet. Early mammals were likely predators, but species have since adapted; carnivores eat animals, herbivores consume plants containing complex carbohydrates like cellulose, and herbivores rely on gut bacteria in a multichambered stomach or large cecum to digest these substances. Some mammals are coprophagous, consuming feces to absorb undigested nutrients. Omnivores eat both plants and animals; carnivores have simple digestive tracts due to the ease of digesting meat, though baleen whales have multi-chambered stomachs like herbivores. Small mammals, weighing less than about 18 ounces (510 g; 1.1 lb), are mostly insectivorous because they cannot sustain a slow herbivorous digestive process; larger mammals can tolerate slower feeding or digestion. Some omnivores show varying degrees of carnivory and herbivory, categorized as mesocarnivory (50–70% meat), hypercarnivory (70% or more meat), or hypocarnivory (50% or less meat), with differences in dentition—hypocarnivores have dull, triangular teeth for grinding, while hypercarnivores have conical, sharp teeth and strong jaws for bone-crushing, as in hyenas, some of which had sabre-shaped canines. Some physiological carnivores consume plant matter and some physiological herbivores consume meat, which from a behavioral standpoint makes them omnivores, but from a physiological perspective, they may still be classified as carnivores or herbivores if they obtain nutrients from non-complementary sources; for example, giraffes, camels, and cattle gnaw bones for minerals, and cats eat grass to expel hairballs, aid hemoglobin production, or act as a laxative. Many mammals hibernate when food is scarce, with larger species like bears becoming polyphagic to build fat stores and smaller ones storing food; during hibernation, metabolism slows, heart and respiratory rates decrease, and internal temperatures drop—Arctic ground squirrels can reach −2.9 °C (26.8 °F), though their heads and necks remain above 0 °C (32 °F). Some mammals in hot environments aestivate during drought or extreme heat, such as the fat-tailed dwarf lemur (Cheirogaleus medius). Terrestrial animals in captivity learn to drink water, but most free-roaming mammals stay hydrated through moisture in food and learn to seek high-fluid foods; drinking methods vary: cats and canines lap with spoon-like tongues, with cats using only the tip of their smooth tongue to pull water into their mouths, while canines use a ladle-like tongue to scoop; ruminants and most herbivores partially submerge their mouths and use a plunging tongue action to draw water; cats drink more slowly than ruminants due to greater predation risks. Desert animals often avoid drinking and rely on succulent plants; in cold environments, hares, tree squirrels, and bighorn sheep consume snow and icicles; giraffes' drinking method, which appears to defy gravity, may involve a plunger-like function of their long necks; elephants draw water into their trunks and squirt it into their mouths. In intelligent mammals like primates, the cerebrum is relatively larger, and intelligence is indicated by learning and behavioral flexibility; rats are considered intelligent due to their ability to learn new tasks, and deer have smaller brains than cats, which must think to outwit prey. Tool use indicates learning and cognition; sea otters use rocks regularly to break open shells, with some populations spending 21% of their time making tools; chimpanzees use twigs to fish for termites, possibly learned through observation and representing true animal teaching; animals may experience a "Eureka moment" when solving puzzles; dogs can also have such moments. Brain size, relative to body mass, is a key indicator of intelligence, with allometric analysis showing brain size scales at approximately the 2⁄3 or 3⁄4 exponent of body mass; the encephalisation quotient compares an animal’s actual brain size to the expected size based on body mass. Sperm whales have the largest brain mass of any animal, averaging 8,000 cubic centimeters (490 cu in) and 7.8 kilograms (17 lb) in mature males. Self-awareness, measured by the mirror test, indicates abstract thinking and is shown in Asian elephants (some pass), chimpanzees, bonobos, orangutans, humans (from 18 months), common bottlenose dolphins, orcas, and false killer whales. Eusociality, the highest level of social organization, involves overlapping generations, division of reproductive labor, and cooperative care of young, typically seen in insects, but also in naked mole-rats and Damaraland mole-rats. Presociality involves communal living, cooperative care, or primitive reproductive division without all three traits of eusociality; humans and some Callitrichidae (marmosets and tamarins) show high levels of cooperative care; Harry Harlow’s 1958 rhesus monkey experiment showed that social interaction is essential for mental and sexual development. Fission–fusion societies change in size and composition, with a parent group splitting into smaller subgroups (fission) or reuniting (fusion) based on environmental or social needs; examples include primates (orangutans, spider monkeys), elephants, spotted hyenas, lions, and dolphins. Solitary animals defend territories and avoid social interactions except during breeding season to prevent resource competition and food depletion; they may also be less conspicuous to predators or prey. In hierarchies, individuals are either dominant or submissive; despotic hierarchies have one dominant individual (e.g., wolves, lemurs), while pecking orders are linear with a top and bottom, sometimes ranked by sex (e.g., hyenas); dominant individuals, or alphas, have high reproductive success, especially in harems where one or a few males have exclusive breeding rights, though non-resident males may be accepted in some cases, such as in common vampire bats. Some mammals are perfectly monogamous, mating for life and not taking other partners, including wolves, Eurasian beavers, and otters. Polygamy occurs in three forms: polygyny (one or multiple dominant males), polyandry (multiple males mating with one female), or polygynandry (multiple males with multiple females); polygyny is the most common, occurring in up to 90% of mammals, excluding leks; lek mating involves males gathering around females and displaying to attract them, as in harbour seals. All higher mammals (excluding monotremes) share live birth and lactation as key adaptations for young care, often building nests or burrows or feeding and guarding offspring for long periods; many are K-selected, investing more time and energy in their young than r-selected animals. When mating, both parents share interest in offspring success, though to varying degrees; mammalian females may exhibit maternal aggression toward other females or their young, though some mammals, like tenrecs, may "aunt" infants; male involvement in child rearing varies by species, such as southern pig-tailed macaques (no care) versus Japanese macaques (care). Non-human mammals play diverse roles in human culture, being the most popular pets with tens of millions of dogs, cats, rabbits, and mice kept globally; mammoths, horses, and deer are among the earliest subjects of art, found in Upper Paleolithic cave paintings like Lascaux; artists such as Albrecht Dürer, George Stubbs, and Edwin Landseer are known for mammal portraits; many species are hunted for sport and food, especially deer and wild boar; horses and dogs are widely raced with betting; there is a tension between animals as companions and as individuals with rights; mammals also play significant roles in literature, film, mythology, and religion.

Dogs, cats, rabbits, and mice are the most popular pets globally, with tens of millions of these animals kept by families worldwide. Mammals like mammoths, horses, and deer have been among the earliest subjects in art, appearing in Upper Paleolithic cave paintings such as at Lascaux. Major artists including Albrecht Dürer, George Stubbs, and Edwin Landseer are renowned for their mammal portraits. Deer and wild boar are especially popular as game animals, and mammals like horses and dogs are widely raced for sport, often involving betting. There is ongoing tension between animals as companions and their status as individuals with rights. Mammals play significant roles in literature, film, mythology, and religion. The domestication of mammals was crucial in the Neolithic transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture and civilization, leading to worldwide societal changes, biodiversity shifts, and environmental transformations. Domestic mammals form a major part of global livestock for meat, including approximately 1.4 billion cattle, 1 billion sheep, 1 billion domestic pigs (as of 2009), and over 700 million rabbits (as of 1985). Cattle and horses have long been used for work and transport, providing about 80% of power for small farms in the developing world and 20% of global transport, primarily in rural areas, with pack animals still used in mountainous regions. Mammal skins produce leather for shoes, clothing, and upholstery, and wool from sheep, goats, and alpacas has been used for centuries in clothing. Mammals are vital in scientific research, especially in genetics and medicine, with millions of mice and rats used annually; knockout mice, genetically modified with inactivated genes, help study gene functions, and non-human primates are used due to their similarity to humans. Despite their benefits, humans have severely impacted wild mammals, with wild mammal biomass now at just 4% of all mammals—96% being humans and their livestock—terrestrial wild mammals making up only 2%. Hybrids result from breeding genetically distinct individuals and include intra-specific (e.g., Bengal and Siberian tigers), interspecific (e.g., lions and tigers), and intergeneric (e.g., sheep and goats) crosses, occurring naturally in hybrid zones; some, like the red wolf, are recognized as species though controversially. Breeding-back efforts attempt to recreate extinct animals, such as Heck cattle resembling the aurochs, but lose the original wildtype gene pool. Purebred wild species face extinction due to genetic pollution—uncontrolled hybridization leading to gene swamping and outcompetition by hybrids—such as the endangered wild water buffalo threatened by domestic water buffalo. Defaunation, driven primarily by human activity, has led to empty forests and loss of large vertebrates, with the Quaternary extinction event suggesting human hunting of megafauna like the woolly mammoth. The IPBES 2019 Global Assessment Report states that wild mammal biomass has declined by 82% since the beginning of human civilization, with wild animals accounting for only 4% of mammalian biomass. Species like rhinoceroses, giraffes, primates, and pangolins are predicted to go extinct soon. The WWF’s 2020 Living Planet Report shows vertebrate wildlife populations have declined by 68% since 1970 due to human activities such as overconsumption, population growth, and intensive farming, indicating a sixth mass extinction. Hunting and poaching threaten hundreds of mammal species, especially near villages, such as peccaries, and the ivory trade severely impacts African elephants. Marine mammals face entanglement in fishing gear, with cetaceans suffering between 65,000 and 86,000 discard mortalities annually. Global conservation efforts include the Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio Accord), with 189 signatory countries, and the IUCN, which has over 1,200 member organizations. Recent extinctions, defined as those after 1500, include around 80 mammal species since that time and 2015. Some species, like the Père David’s deer, are extinct in the wild and survive only in captivity; others, like the Florida panther, are ecologically extinct due to critically low numbers; some are locally extinct (extirpated), such as Atlantic grey whales.
